explanation: Engineer Neil Papworth typed it on a computer and sent it to a Vodafone director's phone during an office Christmas party. Handsets could not yet send texts, so no reply came.

claims.text: The first SMS text message, sent to a mobile phone on 3 December 1992, read 'Merry Christmas'.
The first SMS did not read 'Happy New Year', 'Hello world' or 'Can you hear me?'.
Engineer Neil Papworth sent that message, typing it on a computer.
It was received on the phone of Vodafone director Richard Jarvis, who was at an office Christmas party.
Mobile phones of the time could not send text messages, so Jarvis could not reply.

The search summary states the date, the text and both people plainly with no conflict, but it names its sources only as a group and the list includes Tier C pages (rallypoint, maketecheasier, a podcast blog), so the call counts at Tier C and does not confirm on its own. claimResults.note: Rival test: 'Happy New Year' is the nearest seasonal pull and 'Hello world' tempts programmers, but the recorded text is the Christmas greeting, so all three distractors are wrong. The same search above gives the text as 'Merry Christmas' and nothing else.

claimResults.note: The search summary agrees: Papworth was a developer and test engineer and typed the message on a PC because phones had no keyboards.

evidence.restatement: The handset that got it, an Orbitel 901, belonged to Vodafone's Richard Jarvis, who was at the firm's Christmas party.

claimResults.note: The search summary notes that sources vary on Jarvis's exact title (director, chief engineer, managing director). 'Vodafone director' in the explanation sits inside that range, so it holds; a writer wanting zero exposure could drop the title, but it is not wrong.

evidence.restatement: Phones in 1992 could receive but not compose texts, so Jarvis had no way to answer.

claimResults.note: Papworth has said in interviews that no reply was possible, and the search summary reports that Jarvis did not reply and that phones then had no keyboards.
